children: employees were apparently the target of an alleged Russian spy who had secretly entered the U.S. and was attempting to gather intelligence on the company due to its involvement in the Ukraine-Russian war.

A federal grand jury has indicted Igor D’iu, a Russian national, on charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, acting as an agent of a foreign government without notice to the Attorney General, interstate stalking, and fraud in connection with identification documents, the U.S. Department of Justice announced on Thursday. Although the DOJ did not name the targeted company, NBC reported it was Palantir, citing unnamed sources with knowledge of the investigation.

"As alleged, D’iu entered our country illegally at the direction of foreign handlers to surveil, follow, and gather information about some of those who work in this vital industry," said Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. "Such conduct, if proven, is a flagrant violation of U.S. sovereignty and an unacceptable attempt at intimidation. We will use every tool at our disposal to find, prosecute, and punish such conduct, wherever and whenever it happens."

D’iu traveled from Istanbul, Turkey, to Mexico City, Mexico, in June 2026. From there his co-conspirators connected him with an individual who helped him cross into the U.S., according to the affidavit. Once he arrived, he purchased laptops, cell phones, wireless networking equipment, and remote access software. He also began operating under the false name of Hugo Landry Johns.

From there, he allegedly visited a coffee shop near Palantir's Palo Alto district office. He then attempted to identify company employees and photograph their laptop screens while they worked. He also positioned his laptop at specific locations around the company in an attempt to remotely access information from nearby employee computers.
D’iu then allegedly stepped up his reconnaissance missions, surveilling employee homes and tracking employees by car. At one point he followed an employee for 30 miles.

"D’iu allegedly aggressively continued following her, including through U-turns and illegal left turns, and ran a red light to remain behind her vehicle," according to a DOJ statement. "Fearing for her safety, the employee called 911 and was instructed to drive to the San Francisco Police Department's Mission Station."

In October, the FBI executed search warrants at D’iu's residence in East Palo Alto, where they recovered $18,000 in cash, two laptops, two iPhones, two Russian passports, wireless networking equipment, and the fraudulent identifications. They also discovered a notebook containing personal details of at least three employees.

"Igor D’iu was allegedly recruited, directed, and funded by the Russian government to stalk employees of a major U.S. technology company, using physical surveillance, electronic tracking devices, and fraudulent identities to gather intelligence," said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. "Russia may rely on covert operatives and criminal intermediaries as it attempts to gain an edge in its war against Ukraine, but those tactics do not place its government or its collaborators beyond the reach of the law."
If found guilty, D’iu faces up to 10 years in prison, or more if the punishments are applied consecutively, and more than $500,000 in fines.

title: Palantir workers target of Russian spy; DOJ indicts suspect
